speakerBio: Nephrologist who runs the 'sodium is a water problem' bootcamp and has never met a hyponatraemia she couldn't solve with a serum osmolality, a volume exam, and two spot urine numbers.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 78-year-old woman is admitted from a nursing home, drowsy and confused. Her daughter says she has been "not herself" for three days, unsteady, and had a brief shake of the arms this morning. The bloods land: Na⁺ 112 mmol/L, K⁺ 4.1, urea 3.1, creatinine 62, glucose 6. The FY1 reaches for a bag of 0.9% saline and writes "hyponatraemia — replace sodium." Stop. She does not have a sodium problem. She has a water problem. Before we hang anything, we are going to work the algorithm — serum osmolality, then volume status, then urine osmolality and urine sodium — because getting the mechanism right decides whether we restrict fluid, give saline, or reach for hypertonic saline, and whether we save her brain or infarct it by correcting too fast.

1 · 🧠 Mechanism first — hyponatraemia is (almost always) too much water

The single most important sentence in this talk: the plasma sodium concentration tells you about water, not about sodium. Sodium is a concentration — mmol of sodium per litre of water. You can be hyponatraemic while your total body sodium is high (heart failure), normal (SIADH), or low (diarrhoea). What unites almost every case is an excess of water relative to solute, and the gatekeeper of water excretion is one hormone: antidiuretic hormone (ADH / vasopressin / AVP).

A healthy kidney can dilute urine to ~50 mOsm/kg and excrete 15–20 L of free water a day. To become hyponatraemic you must either (a) drink more water than that maximally dilute kidney can excrete — rare, or (b) far more commonly, be unable to make dilute urine because ADH is switched on. ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct and reabsorbs pure water, concentrating the urine and diluting the plasma.

Hyponatraemia is a disorder of water handling, and the master switch is ADH. Ask of every patient: "why is ADH on, and should it be?"

ADH is released appropriately by two triggers: high plasma osmolality (the osmostat), and — overriding everything — real or perceived low circulating volume (baroreceptor drive). This is why a hypovolaemic patient and an oedematous heart-failure patient (low effective circulating volume) both retain water and both drop their sodium. ADH is released inappropriately — with no osmotic or volume stimulus — in SIADH.

💡 The vicious cycle in the volume-depleted patient

Vomiting and diarrhoea lose salt AND water. The volume loss triggers baroreceptor ADH; the patient, thirsty, drinks water or is given dextrose; ADH holds that water in; sodium falls further. Give salt water (restore volume) and ADH switches off, the kidney dumps the retained free water, and — beware — the sodium can rise dangerously fast. Hold that thought for section 7.

2 · 🗺️ The algorithm — three questions, in order

Every hyponatraemia is solved by three sequential measurements. Do them in order and the diagnosis falls out. The European (ESICM/ESE/ERA-EDTA 2014) guideline is built on exactly this spine.

  1. Serum osmolality — is this true hypotonic hyponatraemia, or a lab artefact / another solute? Excludes pseudohyponatraemia and hyperglycaemic (translocational) hyponatraemia.
  2. Volume status — clinically, is the patient hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, or hypervolaemic (oedematous)? This splits the differential into three buckets.
  3. Urine osmolality and urine sodium — the kidney's testimony: is ADH on, and is the kidney holding or wasting sodium?
Serum osmolality → volume status → urine osmolality + urine sodium. Never skip a step; each one closes off half the differential.

3 · 💧 Step 1 — serum osmolality: is it real?

Measured serum osmolality (or calculated: 2×Na⁺ + glucose + urea, all mmol/L) sorts hyponatraemia into three tonicities:

Serum osmolalityCategoryWhat is going on
Normal (275–295)Pseudohyponatraemia (isotonic)Lab artefact — severe hyperlipidaemia or paraproteinaemia (myeloma) displaces plasma water; the analyser reports a falsely low Na⁺. The real plasma-water sodium is normal.
High (>295)Translocational (hypertonic)An extra osmole pulls water OUT of cells into plasma, diluting sodium: hyperglycaemia (DKA/HHS) or mannitol. Real, but the treatment is the glucose, not the sodium.
Low (<275)True hypotonic hyponatraemiaThe one we care about. Proceed to volume status. Everything below is about this group.
💡 The hyperglycaemia correction

Add ~2.4 mmol/L to the measured sodium for every 10 mmol/L (≈180 mg/dL) that glucose is above normal (~5.5). A patient with glucose 45 and "sodium 125" actually has a corrected sodium of ~135 — they are not hyponatraemic at all once the glucose is treated. Correct the maths before you correct the patient.

⚠️ Don't be fooled by a normal osmolality

A hyponatraemic patient with a normal measured osmolality has pseudohyponatraemia — a spurious result from lipids or paraprotein. Treating this "hyponatraemia" with saline or fluid restriction harms a patient whose real sodium is fine. Always confirm true hypotonicity before you act. Ask the lab for a direct ion-selective electrode reading if you suspect it.

4 · 🩺 Step 2 — volume status: the clinical fork

This is the hardest and most important bedside judgement in the algorithm, and the European guideline is candid that clinical volume assessment is imperfect — but it drives the whole differential. Examine JVP, skin turgor, mucous membranes, postural BP/pulse, oedema, and review the fluid balance and weight chart.

BucketTotal body sodiumTotal body waterClinical signs
Hypovolaemic↓↓ (lost more Na than water)↓Dry mucosae, ↓skin turgor, ↓JVP, postural drop, tachycardia, oliguria
Euvolaemic~Normal↑ (mildly)No oedema, no dehydration — looks "well" volume-wise. The SIADH bucket.
Hypervolaemic (oedematous)↑ (but low effective circulating volume)↑↑Peripheral/pulmonary oedema, raised JVP, ascites — heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
🎯 "Effective" circulating volume — why the oedematous patient retains water

The heart-failure or cirrhotic patient is drowning in total-body salt and water, yet the arterial baroreceptors sense underfilling (poor forward output, splanchnic vasodilatation). The body reads this as hypovolaemia and switches on ADH and aldosterone — so it retains yet more water, diluting sodium further. The paradox: total body water is high, but the neurohormonal signal is "I am empty." This is why we restrict fluid and treat the heart/liver, not give saline.

5 · 🔬 Step 3 — urine osmolality & urine sodium: the kidney's confession

Two spot urine numbers, taken together, confirm the mechanism the exam suggested.

Urine osmolality — is ADH on?

  • Urine osmolality < 100 mOsm/kg = maximally dilute urine = ADH is appropriately OFF. The kidney is doing its job dumping free water; the problem is pure water excess overwhelming a normal kidney → primary polydipsia, low-solute intake ("beer potomania" / "tea-and-toast"), or reset osmostat. These do not need saline — they need the water/solute problem fixed.
  • Urine osmolality > 100 (usually >300) mOsm/kg = urine inappropriately concentrated = ADH is ON. Now the urine sodium tells you why.

Urine sodium — is the kidney holding or wasting salt?

  • Urine Na⁺ < 30 mmol/L = kidney is avidly reabsorbing sodium = it senses low effective circulating volume → hypovolaemia (GI losses, poor intake) OR an oedematous state (heart failure, cirrhosis). The clinical volume exam distinguishes these two.
  • Urine Na⁺ > 30 mmol/L (with euvolaemia and normal renal/adrenal/thyroid function) = kidney is NOT volume-avid = the classic fingerprint of SIADH. Also seen in renal salt wasting, diuretics, and adrenal insufficiency.
Urine osmolality asks "is ADH on?"; urine sodium asks "does the body think it is volume-depleted?" Together they name the cause.
⚠️ Diuretics wreck the urine sodium

A patient on a thiazide is the great confounder: thiazides impair urinary dilution and cause classic hyponatraemia, but they also make the urine sodium high, mimicking SIADH. You cannot interpret urine electrolytes reliably on diuretics. Stop the thiazide, and remember thiazide-induced hyponatraemia — especially in small, elderly women — is common and can be profound.

6 · 📋 The three buckets — causes by mechanism

Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (low Na, low water; ADH volume-driven)

  • Renal losses (urine Na >30): diuretics (esp. thiazides), cerebral/renal salt wasting, mineralocorticoid deficiency (Addison's), osmotic diuresis.
  • Extra-renal losses (urine Na <30): vomiting, diarrhoea, "third-spacing" (pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, burns), sweating.

Euvolaemic hyponatraemia — SIADH and mimics

SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion. The Bartter & Schwartz criteria (still the reference standard, echoed by the European guideline):

Essential SIADH criterionValue
True hypotonic hyponatraemiaSerum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg
Inappropriately concentrated urineUrine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg
Clinical euvolaemiaNo oedema, no hypovolaemia
Elevated urine sodium on normal salt/water intakeUrine Na⁺ > 30 mmol/L
Normal thyroid & adrenal functionExclude hypothyroidism & hypocortisolism
No recent diuretics—

Supportive: low serum urate and low urea (dilution + increased urate clearance). Causes of SIADH — the four buckets:

  • Malignancy — small-cell lung cancer (ectopic ADH), head & neck, others.
  • Pulmonary — pneumonia, TB, empyema, positive-pressure ventilation.
  • CNS — stroke, subarachnoid/subdural haemorrhage, meningitis, trauma, tumour.
  • Drugs — SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, cyclophosphamide, PPIs, thiazides, MDMA/ecstasy, desmopressin.
🎯 Always check cortisol and thyroid before you call it SIADH

Two great mimics of SIADH present as euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine: adrenal insufficiency (cortisol deficiency → unrestrained ADH) and severe hypothyroidism. Missing an Addisonian crisis and treating it as SIADH with fluid restriction can kill. A short Synacthen test and TSH belong in every euvolaemic hyponatraemia work-up.

Hypervolaemic (oedematous) hyponatraemia

  • Congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome — low effective circulating volume drives ADH; urine Na <30 (except in advanced renal failure or on diuretics).
  • Advanced renal failure — kidney cannot excrete a water load; urine Na may be >30.

7 · 🚨 Acute & symptomatic — the true emergency

Now the split that decides everything: how symptomatic, and how acute? Symptoms come from cerebral oedema — water follows the osmotic gradient into brain cells. The brain adapts over ~48h by extruding solutes, so acute hyponatraemia (<48h — post-op, marathon, MDMA, self-induced water intoxication) is far more dangerous than chronic, because the brain has had no time to adapt.

SeverityFeaturesAction
Severe symptomsSeizures, coma (GCS drop), obtundation, vomiting, cardiorespiratory distressHypertonic (3%) saline NOW — do not wait for the cause
Moderate symptomsConfusion, headache, drowsiness, nauseaPrompt treatment, cause-directed; consider hypertonic saline
Mild / asymptomaticBiochemical finding onlyDiagnose the cause; treat by bucket; correct slowly
⚠️ Severe symptoms = 3% saline, regardless of the cause or the chronicity

A seizing or comatose hyponatraemic patient is dying of cerebral oedema. The European guideline is explicit: give 150 mL of 3% hypertonic saline (or 2 mL/kg) IV over 10–20 minutes, check the sodium, and repeat the bolus up to twice more until symptoms improve or the sodium has risen by 5 mmol/L. The immediate target is a 5 mmol/L rise — that small bump reverses herniation. Do not try to normalise the sodium; you are buying brain, not fixing biochemistry.

The bolus protocol (ESICM/ESE/ERA-EDTA):

  1. 150 mL 3% saline over 10–20 min.
  2. Recheck sodium after 20 min; give a second 150 mL bolus if symptoms persist.
  3. Aim for a 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour, then STOP the boluses.
  4. Once symptoms resolve, switch to slow, cause-directed management and — critically — cap the total 24-hour rise (section 8, and all of session 10).

8 · 🐌 Chronic & asymptomatic — treat the bucket, correct slowly

For chronic hyponatraemia (or after the acute emergency is controlled), the treatment is mechanism-directed, and the golden rule is slow correction:

BucketFirst-line treatmentWhy
Hypovolaemic0.9% saline to restore volumeRestores volume → switches ADH off → kidney excretes free water. Watch for overshoot as ADH turns off.
Euvolaemic (SIADH)Fluid restriction (typically <800–1000 mL/day); treat the cause; ± oral urea / salt+loop; tolvaptan in selected casesRemove the excess water the kidney cannot. Saline can paradoxically worsen SIADH.
HypervolaemicFluid restriction + treat the organ (loop diuretic, HF/cirrhosis therapy)Total body water is already high — do not add salt water.
⚠️ Never give normal saline in SIADH — the "desalination" trap

In SIADH the urine is highly concentrated (say 600 mOsm/kg). Give 0.9% saline (308 mOsm/L): the kidney, driven by ADH, excretes the salt in a small volume of concentrated urine and retains the free water — the sodium can fall further. Saline is the wrong tool for SIADH; the answer is water restriction (and if that fails, a vaptan or oral urea).

Tolvaptan — the vaptan's place

Tolvaptan is a selective oral V2-receptor antagonist ("aquaretic"): it blocks ADH at the collecting duct, producing electrolyte-free water excretion and raising sodium. It works in euvolaemic and hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (SALT-1/SALT-2 trials showed it raises sodium in SIADH and heart failure). Caveats that keep it a specialist drug:

  • Must be started in hospital with 6–8 hourly sodium monitoring — it can correct dangerously fast (overcorrection → ODS risk).
  • Do NOT fluid-restrict simultaneously when initiating — allow the patient to drink to thirst, or correction overshoots.
  • Avoid in liver disease (hepatotoxicity; not for SIADH in cirrhosis at high dose).
  • Reserved for SIADH resistant to fluid restriction, or symptomatic euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia — not first-line.

9 · ⛔ Correction limits — the set-up for session 10

Chronic hyponatraemia is dangerous to have, but even more dangerous to fix too fast. Correcting the sodium faster than the brain can re-accumulate its lost osmolytes causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) — a devastating, often irreversible pontine and extrapontine demyelination. The whole of session 10 is devoted to this, but the numbers you must burn in now:

Limit the rise to ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and ≤ 8 mmol/L per 24 h in high-risk patients (many centres cap at 6–8/24h). Set alarms; recheck sodium every 2–4 h during active correction.
🎯 The high-risk patient (preview of session 10)

ODS risk soars when the sodium is ≤105 mmol/L, or the patient has alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, or liver disease. In these patients aim for the lowest safe rise (~6/24h) and be ready to re-lower the sodium with dextrose ± desmopressin if you overshoot. Correcting our opening patient (Na 112, chronic, elderly) too quickly could leave her locked-in. We will dissect exactly how not to do that next session.

10 · 🧭 Master algorithm — hyponatraemia at a glance

StepTestResultConclusion / next
1Serum osmolalityNormalPseudohyponatraemia (lipids/paraprotein) — STOP
1Serum osmolalityHighHyperglycaemia/mannitol — correct glucose, apply Na correction
1Serum osmolalityLow (<275)True hypotonic — go to step 2
2Volume statusHypovolaemic→ urine Na: <30 extra-renal loss; >30 renal/diuretic/Addison. Rx 0.9% saline
2Volume statusEuvolaemicUrine osm >100 & urine Na >30 → SIADH (exclude thyroid/adrenal). Rx fluid restriction ± tolvaptan
2Volume statusHypervolaemicHF/cirrhosis/nephrotic — urine Na usually <30. Rx fluid restriction + treat organ
3Urine osmolality<100ADH off → primary polydipsia / low-solute (beer potomania). Rx address water/solute
—SeveritySeizure/coma3% saline 150 mL over 10–20 min, target +5 mmol/L, cap ≤10/24h
☠️ M&M — the "tea-and-toast" lady who seized on saline

An 82-year-old widow living alone was admitted with Na⁺ 108, confused. She ate almost nothing but toast and sweet tea — very low solute intake, so her kidney had almost no osmoles to carry free water out ("tea-and-toast / beer-potomania" physiology; urine osmolality was 90, urine Na low). The admitting team, pattern-matching "low sodium = give saline," ran 0.9% saline at 125 mL/h overnight. By morning her sodium had leapt from 108 to 124 — 16 mmol/L in under 12 hours. Because restoring solute and volume switched off her ADH, she poured out litres of dilute urine and her sodium auto-corrected on top of the saline. Three days later she became dysarthric, then quadriparetic and mute: osmotic demyelination syndrome. Lessons: (1) low-solute hyponatraemia needs cautious solute/volume repletion, not brisk saline; (2) once ADH switches off the sodium can run away on its own — you must anticipate and cap it; (3) she was high-risk (elderly, malnourished, sodium far below 110); the target should have been ≤6–8 mmol/L in 24h with 2-hourly monitoring and pre-emptive desmopressin. The team fixed the number and infarcted the brainstem. This is why session 10 exists.

11 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Hyponatraemia is a water problem, not a salt problem — ask "why is ADH on?" for every patient.
  2. Work the algorithm in order: serum osmolality (exclude pseudo- and hyperglycaemic) → volume status → urine osmolality + urine sodium.
  3. Correct glucose first — add ~2.4 mmol/L to sodium per 10 mmol/L glucose above normal.
  4. SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion (euvolaemic, urine osm >100, urine Na >30, normal thyroid & adrenal, no diuretics) — treat with fluid restriction, not saline.
  5. Match treatment to the bucket: hypovolaemic → saline; euvolaemic → restrict ± tolvaptan; hypervolaemic → restrict + treat the organ.
  6. Severe symptoms (seizure/coma) = 3% saline 150 mL over 10–20 min, repeat to a 5 mmol/L rise — buy brain first.
  7. Cap the correction: ≤10 mmol/L/24h (≤8, aim 6, in high-risk). Overcorrection causes osmotic demyelination — the subject of session 10.

moderatorQs.q: A euvolaemic patient has Na 124, urine osmolality 480, urine Na 55, and is on no diuretics. The FY1 diagnoses SIADH. What must you check before accepting that?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion, and two great mimics present identically — as euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and high urine sodium: adrenal insufficiency (cortisol deficiency releases the brake on ADH) and severe hypothyroidism. Before labelling this SIADH I would check a 9am cortisol / short Synacthen test and TSH, confirm true hypotonicity (serum osmolality <275), and be sure there is no occult diuretic or recent thiazide. Missing an Addisonian crisis and 'treating the SIADH' with fluid restriction can be fatal. Only once thyroid and adrenal axes are normal and the Bartter–Schwartz criteria are met is it SIADH — then hunt the cause (malignancy, pulmonary, CNS, drugs).

moderatorQs.q: Why is giving 0.9% saline to a patient with SIADH sometimes actively harmful?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because of desalination. In SIADH the urine is intensely concentrated (say 600 mOsm/kg) because ADH is fixed 'on'. If you infuse 0.9% saline (308 mOsm/L of solute in 1 litre of water), the kidney — still under ADH — excretes that sodium load in a smaller volume of concentrated urine and retains the free water. The net effect can be a fall in serum sodium. The rule of thumb: if the urine osmolality exceeds the osmolality of the fluid you are giving, saline makes SIADH worse. The correct treatment is to remove water — fluid restriction, and if refractory, oral urea or a vaptan such as tolvaptan.

moderatorQs.q: A patient with chronic hyponatraemia at Na 110 seizes. Walk me through the immediate management and the ceiling on correction.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A seizing hyponatraemic patient is dying of cerebral oedema and needs hypertonic saline immediately, irrespective of chronicity. Per the European guideline: 150 mL of 3% saline (or ~2 mL/kg) IV over 10–20 minutes, recheck sodium at 20 minutes, and repeat the bolus up to twice until the seizure stops or the sodium has risen by 5 mmol/L — that small rise is enough to reverse herniation. Then STOP the boluses and switch to slow, cause-directed care. Crucially, because this is chronic hyponatraemia the brain has adapted, so the 24-hour ceiling is tight: ≤10 mmol/L in 24h, and ≤8 (aiming ~6) in high-risk patients (Na ≤105, alcohol, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease). Recheck every 2 hours and be prepared to re-lower with dextrose ± desmopressin if it overshoots.

audienceQs.q: My patient has Na 125 but a glucose of 40. Do I need to treat the sodium?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Almost certainly not directly — this is translocational (hypertonic) hyponatraemia. The high glucose is an extra osmole that pulls water out of cells into the plasma, diluting the measured sodium. Correct it on paper: add roughly 2.4 mmol/L to the sodium for every 10 mmol/L of glucose above ~5.5. Here glucose is ~35 above normal, so add about +8 → a corrected sodium of ~133. The patient is essentially normonatraemic; the treatment is fluids and insulin for the hyperglycaemia (DKA/HHS), and the sodium will look after itself as the glucose falls. Watch the sodium rise as glucose comes down, and factor that into your fluid choice.

audienceQs.q: We're about to start tolvaptan on a patient with SIADH. What safety points should I flag to the team?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Several. Tolvaptan is a potent V2-antagonist aquaretic and can raise the sodium too fast, risking osmotic demyelination. So: it must be initiated in hospital with sodium checked every 6–8 hours for the first day or two; the patient should NOT be fluid-restricted at initiation — let them drink to thirst, or the correction overshoots; start at the lowest dose (15 mg). Flag hepatotoxicity — avoid in liver disease and check LFTs; it is not used in high dose for cirrhosis-related hyponatraemia. It is reserved for SIADH resistant to fluid restriction or symptomatic euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia — not first line. Have a plan (dextrose ± desmopressin) ready in case correction exceeds ~8–10 mmol/L in 24h.

audienceQs.q: How do I actually use the urine osmolality and urine sodium together — which do I look at first?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Read them as two separate questions. Urine osmolality answers 'is ADH switched on?' — if it is <100 mOsm/kg the urine is maximally dilute, ADH is appropriately off, and you are dealing with pure water excess (primary polydipsia, low-solute 'tea-and-toast'/beer potomania) — no saline needed. If it is >100 (usually >300), ADH is on, and you move to the second number. Urine sodium answers 'does the body think it's volume-depleted?' — <30 mmol/L means the kidney is avidly holding salt (true hypovolaemia or an oedematous low-effective-volume state), while >30 in a euvolaemic patient off diuretics is the fingerprint of SIADH. Remember diuretics and any recent thiazide invalidate the urine sodium entirely.
